in making both ends meet. A saving of twenty-five dollars would have meant a great deal to him.
I should also like to remind my Ontario farm friends that we in the west pay out in freight nine cents out of eveiy dollar expended in the purchase of farm implements, and that in itself is sufficient to make or unmake the farmer.
I would also remind the house of another condition in the west from which we suffer. We are marooned in the heart of a great continent, far removed from tide-water, with a long rail haul and high freight rates, and freight rates have been increased about 50 per cent in the last few years. If, in addition to long rail haul and the high freight rates, we have the cost of maintaining the industrialists of eastern Canada, it becomes a very heavy burden indeed. We have to compete in the open markets of the world when we sell our products. We compete with the Argentine, where labour is practically all native or peon, working for a few cents a day, and where I understand the farms are located pretty much on the great rivers that traverse that South American country, and a great deal of the grain is delivered on flat bottom boats which carry it to tide-water at a low rate. In any event there would be only a short rail haul. We have also to compete with Russia, with its state labour. We have to compete with the outside world in everything we sell. We sell in the lowest market, in the open markets of the world, but when we buy our implements and other necessities we must buy in the most highly protected market of the world. This makes it very, very difficult for the people of western Canada particularly to carry on under such trade arrangements.
I might remind the house that when we sell our wheat we must pay the freight to tide-water, and the average freight rate on wheat from prairie points is eighteen cents a bushel. There was a time for several years from 1931 to 1933, inclusive, when the price of wheat in western Canada averaged forty to fifty cents a bushel, and to have to deduct eighteen cents from that amount for freight alone it was an extremely serious matter for the farmer.
I should like to say further, in my condemnation of the system of bonusing the industrialists, that perhaps we have built up a false state of society; perhaps we have, through the bonus system, raised the cost of living in our cities to the point where it is -necessary to maintain a very high price level for manufactured goods. I spend some of

my weekends motoring through good old Ontario. I do so for the purpose of information. I like Ontario and its people and the countryside, but it grieves me very much when I see the dilapidated farm homes and the number of abandoned farms. Then I drive into one of your industrial centres, small or large, and there I see an almost vulgar display of wealth, in the form of luxurious homes, housing perhaps the owners of these factories, with their yachts on the St. Lawrence river or lake Ontario, and two or three cars, simply living in the lap of luxury while the whole countryside around them, the very market for their products, going down and down and down. I made a trip through Huron county not so long ago. And I do not wonder that the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) makes the speeches he does in the house. On one road I counted five farms one after the other with good buildings, brick or stone houses, big barns, but nobody living on any one of those farms. Why? They had all moved into the cities because of the unnatural conditions created there through the bonus system. What the end will be here in Ontario I do not know, but I think it may be even worse for us in the west.
I am not surprised at what has happened politically in Alberta in recent years. Do not forget that in Alberta the freight rate alone on wheat-my Alberta friends will correct me if I am wrong-averages nineteen cents a bushel from points in central Alberta to the head- of the lakes. How could they carry on under those circumstances and pay the prices they have to pay for the goods they have to buy? I believe the Canadian farmer is the most industrious and intelligent man to be found in any part of the whole world-, and if he is given an even break, if he is given the privilege of buying in the same market in which he sells, if he is given the privilege to buy at world prices, he will be able to compete with any country in the world. But the dice are loaded against him. Under present conditions he cannot compete in the markets of the world. How can he, when he has to pay around 50 or 60 per cent more for his goods than he would have to pay if it were not for the tariff? I have before me an invoice of goods imported into Canada within the last few days. It covers a shipment of cotton underwear, and what could be more universal than that? The tariff has been reduced considerably on cotton underwear since the present government has come into office; but I find that on this shipment of goods, the price was raised -by the time it reached the ultimate

I am very glad the minister has raised that point, because in my computation I took the price paid for the goods, the original cost plus the duty; I added to that the excise tax; I added the sales tax; then I added the profit taken between the custom house and the consumer, and it amounted to about 65 per cent of the original cost.
After all, the duty does not end at the boundary; it just nicely begins there. That is the point which I believe we have been missing, quite innocently, but the impost goes on until it reaches the consumer. If I am in business and I invest SI,000 in goods in the United States and I have to invest S200 more when they reach the boundary, I am going to add my profit to the $1,200 and not to the $1,000 only. So the impost continues, as I have said, until it reaches the consumer; we must get that point clear in our minds. That is why the country is going down as it is, while our cities build up. I am astonished that our leading statesmen are not more alarmed at what is happening in this regard. One cannot go around the country and see barn doors falling off, gates hanging on one hinge, buildings which have not been painted for the last fifteen years, and half the farm, if it is occupied at all, seeded down to grass because the farmer cannot afford to operate it, without realizing that we cannot have such conditions and maintain a healthy country society. Perhaps by reason of the bonus system, we have built up a false social structure in our large industrial centres. What I should like to see is the creation of conditions in this country which would make it so attractive to our young people that they would want to live on farms. We must find some means of attracting our people to the farms in greater numbers.
I might remark here that until recently we in the west regarded ourselves as being in the heart of a great continent, but within the last few years we have been brought a little closer to tide-water through the port of Churchill. Very little, however, has been done to encourage trade through that port. I am sorry the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), who represents that constituency, is not in the house, because I should like to suggest to him that the establishment of a bonded warehouse at Churchill would do a great deal to encourage trade
through that port. Many heavy commodities like binder twine, plate glass, barbed wire, rolling mill products and china, of which we import a great deal, could come in through that port at a great saving to the west. It is a thousand miles closer than Montreal to the centre of consumption in the west, and I believe it could be used by the producers of those commodities in countries like Holland, Belgium, France and Great Britain, which export them to Canada. The farmer needs his binder twine in April and May, in any event not later than June and July, and not in August and September, when ships come into Churchill. The hardware man wants his glass in March and April, not in the fall. There are many commodities which could be brought into Churchill if we had a bonded warehouse there. I think in that way we could do something to encourage the importation of goods required in the west.
I have under my hand a statement of the freight rates actually paid at the present time, showing the savings that could be effected if we could use Churchill to a greater extent than we are doing to-day. For example, the freight on a carload of poultry from Dauphin, which is a central point in Manitoba, to Churchill, would cost $262. That same carload shipped to Montreal would cost $457 at present freight rates. To ship a carload of eggs from Dauphin to Montreal costs $394; it would cost $264 if routed via Churchill. Remember that Churchill is the same distance from the markets of Europe as is Montreal. I could mention many other lommodities. Take cattle; the freight rate on a carload from Dauphin to Montreal is $191, whereas the rate to Churchill is $102, or a saving of $89. That is a considerable amount when one does not get very much for the cattle anyway. I sincerely hope the government will give serious consideration to the suggestion to establish a bonded warehouse in Churchill.
In the course of this debate reference was made to the help given to the west by eastern Canada. I want to assure eastern members- although, thank God, I do not live in the dried-out area-that there is no one more grateful than I have been for the very generous assistance given to the west by the people of eastern Canada, in contributing, as they did, more than a hundred carloads of fruit and vegetables last year to the dried-out area, and we are also grateful to parliament for the money voted to assist the people in those localities. But I took the trouble the other day to get from the statistical branch the value of agricultural production of the three prairie provinces in the

Farm Implements Committee Report
last twenty years, and I received these staggering figures. We produced agricultural products in the three prairie provinces to the value of $70,115,000,000. We may very properly ask, What has become of that seventy billions? You will find, if you go around Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, Brantford and all the other industrial centres of eastern Canada, a great deal of it. It is very difficult for us to calculate just how much of that seventy billions of dollars has gone to the upbuilding of Toronto. I believe that if it had not been for the west Toronto would be a little straggling city of not more than two hundred to two hundred and fifty thousand, and Hamilton would be no more than a good sized town, because seventy-five per cent of the products of these cities have gone west of the great lakes.

subtopic: PROPOSED APPLICATION OP CROWSNEST PASS RATES ON GRAIN WESTWARD AS WELL AS EASTWARD

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, March 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Reid for the second reading of Bill No. 18, to amend the Railway Act (rates on grain).

subtopic: PROPOSED APPLICATION OP CROWSNEST PASS RATES ON GRAIN WESTWARD AS WELL AS EASTWARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I moved the adjournment of the debate on this motion on March 11. Nearly two months have passed, and I regret that a bill as important as this one has taken so long to reach this stage. I trust that the house will facilitate the passage of this bill. I would suggest that the government take it over and have the railway commission deal with it accordingly.
On three occasions, twice during the former parliament and once in 1936, I moved resolutions that, had they met with the approval of the house, would have meant reductions in the domestic freight rates, similar to what is being provided for by this bill. On one occasion I secured from the then Minister of Railways and Canals, the Hon. Doctor Manion, a promise that he would recommend to the board of railway commissioners the bringing into force of an agreement between the provinces and the railways to provide for a reduction in domestic rates going westward. This agreement came into force on March 10, 1937, to cover movements from points on the prairies to the Fraser valley and the British Columbia coast. This was covered by tariff item 145, C.R.C. 154. It effected a reduction in the domestic rate from Edmonton and Calgary to Vancouver from 41^ cents to 30 cents per 100 pounds. However, this arrangement lasted only a few months.

subtopic: PROPOSED APPLICATION OP CROWSNEST PASS RATES ON GRAIN WESTWARD AS WELL AS EASTWARD
speechtext: Why was it discontinued?

subtopic: PROPOSED APPLICATION OP CROWSNEST PASS RATES ON GRAIN WESTWARD AS WELL AS EASTWARD
speechtext:
I think the submission was made by the railway companies to the board of railway commissioners that the rates were not profitable, and the previous rates were

restored. On the occasions I have mentioned, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), who introduced this bill, did not support my resolution. However, he continued to introduce a bill each year calling for a reduction in freight rates. The argument which has been advanced against his bills is that their passage would upset the whole freight rate structure. That argument has always been presented when any attempt has been made to obtain a reduction in domestic rates. This bill is similar in principle to my resolution and I propose to support it.
As I stated a moment ago, this bill deals with a special class of freight, and its acceptance would not upset the freight rate structure. The poultrymen, the dairymen and the stockmen of British Columbia would benefit materially if it were accepted, and the grain growers on the prairies would also be assisted by having access to an increased market in British Columbia for coarse grains. Many different organizations in western Canada, particularly farm organizations, have passed from time to time resolutions which have been presented to parliament asking for a reduction in domestic rates.
It is not necessary to-night to burden the house with comparisons of rates. The hon. member who sponsors this bill has covered that matter quite well. He has dealt with rates in both eastern and western Canada, and I think the figures he placed on Hansard make out a good case for his bill. However, I should like to direct attention to the rates which apply from Indian Head, Saskatchewan, near to my home town, to Vancouver. The domestic rate is 52 J cents, and the export rate 27 cents per 100 pounds. I claim that is an unjust rate and the producers have cause for complaint.
The hon. member, when speaking to his bill, mentioned that some three and a half million bushels or more did go from the prairie provinces to British Columbia under these present rates and that the consumers in British Columbia paid nearly $450,000 more in freight rates than they would have done had the rates prevailed that he is asking for in his bill.
I wish to deal briefly with the question of corn. Com is imported into British Columbia and is used there for feed purposes by the poultry producers and dairymen. It is estimated that com equal to about 1,500 cars of barley is imported into British Columbia each year. That is a very considerable market if we had it for coarse grains, and I think we can prove that coarse grains are equal in food value to com. Experiments have been carried

Railway Act-Grain Rates
on at different experimental stations to ascertain the feed value of corn and barley, and in practically every instance barley has been proven equal to if not better than corn for feeding hogs, beef and dairy cattle and poultry. So, if the western producers could get a market there for their coarse grains, barley and oats, there would not be any loss to the British Columbia producers so far as feed value is concerned.
Parliament, I admit, is not a rate fixing body. I remember that in the former parliament we were always confronted with the argument that we must not do anything to upset the whole freight rate structure, but I claim that the rate I have cited to-night from the central part of Saskatchewan to Vancouver is discriminatory and unjust in its present application.
For the information of members of the house who were not in the former parliament I want to quote from a decision given by the board of railway commissioners in 1922. The late Hon. Frank Oliver, in giving a dissenting judgment to the decision given by the board of railway commissioners in that year, said:
There should not be any differential at all, especially on coarse grains and low grade wheat going to British Columbia.
I think that is a pretty fair argument. I have already mentioned that we might get a market in British Columbia for some 1,500 carloads of barley alone, and at thirty cents per 100 pounds that would mean 8220,000 for the railway company taking it through the mountains into British Columbia. I may point out that the railway companies do not derive any great revenue from the freight on corn. Corn comes in by vessels, and while it is distributed by the railways to the interior, the rail haul is short and does not provide a great revenue for the railway companies. On different occasions the railway companies have said they were willing to assist, and I think we should give them an opportunity to do so.
Prior to 1897 we had a rate on grains to Fort William from the province of Saskatchewan and western points of about two cents less than the present rate. For example, the freight from Indian Head to Fort William was seventeen cents per 100 pounds. At the present time we are paying nineteen cents, and the farmers cannot understand why in this day and age, with all the improved transportation facilities that we have, with large engines hauling twice the number of cars, of twice the capacity, and the same crew operating the train, they have to pay more than they did twenty or thirty years ago. I
think the farmers of western Canada are justified in feeling that way about it. If we had the rate reduced to what it was prior to the Crowsnest rates, it would mean a saving to the farmers of the west of about three or four million dollars in freight on their wheat alone, and I think we should have that low rate restored.
I shall not take up very much more time, but before closing I would say that freight rates are of such importance that they should be considered with respect to other commodities than grain. I think we should have a considerable reduction in the freight rate on implements going west, particularly in the carload rates. We have heard a great deal in the house within the last day or two with respect to the prices paid by the western farmer for farm implements, and I heard the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood) say this afternoon that he had used a binder on his farm for thirty years. When one considers the increase in the price of binders, it would not bother him very much if he had to buy only one in thirty years; but if we had a reduction in the freight rate on implements going into western Canada it would be of great value to our farmers, and I think our time could have been better spent within the last day or two if we had been discussing something along that line.
I would also mention the freight rate on coal. I think there should be an adjustment in that rate, particularly from point to point in the western provinces.
Bill No. 31, which has been presented to the house, is now before a special committee. Certain sections of that bill dealing with rates are objectionable, particularly the one dealing with agreed charges. I consider that dangerous, and I hope, when the bill comes back to the house, that provision will have been struck out. I know the farmers of western Canada are anxious that no measure should pass the house containing a provision which would make it possible in any shape or form to establish a monopoly in rates in any commodity. They are anxious that no bill should come into effect that would mean an increase in either the outgoing rates from the prairie provinces or the incoming rates, and I hope, when that bill returns to the house, it will have been so amended that such a thing is not likely to happen. In due course I trust we shall also get a very substantial reduction in the rates on grain, implements and coal.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I trust that the hon. member who has introduced this bill will see fit this year not to withdraw it, as he did on former occasions. It is true the bill
Railway Act-Grain Rates

did not get very far in other sessions, and was finally withdrawn by the hon. member, but I would suggest that this year he endeavour to have the government take over the measure and push it through. I understand that during the campaign in 1935 he assured the electors in the province of British Columbia that if there were a change of government and his party came into power, there would be no difficulty in having the government accept his biil or bring in a similar measure.

speechtext: This parliament is a legislative body, and I have always contended that as far as possible we in our capacity as members of this house should refrain from becoming an administrative body. There are few lion, members, I care not in what part of the house they sit, who can discuss the subject of freight rates with any degree of understanding in so far as the dominion is concerned. I know very little about it, and I think the same is true of many other hon. members. In previous years I have invariably contended so far as a bill of this kind is concerned that, while there may be a good deal of merit in the contentions of the hon. member who sponsors it, the principle is one which I cannot support. The proper principle to follow is that this parliament should not be a rate fixing body. The moment we start fixing freight rates I do not know where we are going to start and where we are going to end. I would far sooner leave the matter to a body properly constituted and created for that particular purpose. I do not know whether the railway commission are making a good job or a bad job of fixing freight rates.

subtopic: PROPOSED APPLICATION OP CROWSNEST PASS RATES ON GRAIN WESTWARD AS WELL AS EASTWARD
speechtext: If they are not, the proper course is to change the personnel of the commission and not to let us as members of parliament become involved in creating a rate structure of which we know very little. There may be a hardship involved in what the hon. member has stated, and nobody yet so far as I know has explained the reason for this differential between export and local rates. It is quite possible that the export rate is far too low, and I have been wondering whether, if the export rate were raised to the level of the domestic rate, that would satisfy hon. members from British Columbia. The fact that the export rate was reduced to a very low level, perhaps, for competitive purposes, may not be altogether a good reason for bringing the domestic rate down, although there may -be some grounds for it. My contention, which I have previously maintained in the house, is that as a member with very little knowledge of the freight rate structure I am not, if I can possibly avoid it, going to be a party to fixing freight rates in any part of the dominion. On the other hand, if perhaps there is fault to be found with the composition of the railway commission or if they are not doing their job properly, the remedy is, not to attack the freight rate structure but to attack the railway commission and change its membership.

This bill has been before parliament each year since 1933, and, I believe, almost everything that requires to be said on the subject has been said. I can only reiterate what I have said each time when the bill has been discussed, namely, that the consideration of freight -rates, being a highly technical matter, is one for the board of railway commissioners and not for parliament. I think parliament has acted on freight rates only twice since the board of railway commissioners was established. On both those occasions parliament acted because a change was to be effected in a statutory rate and the change could be effected only by statute. The Crowsnest pass rates were established in 1897. The rates were changed in the early years of the war, having been an intolerable burden on the railways under the stress of those days, and after the war parliament acted again to restore the Crowsnest rates. We all start from the position that the Crowsnest rates are adequate, representing a fair return to the railways for a given service. That, of course, is entirely erroneous. If we could restore the other conditions of 1897, rates of pay, prices of equipment and supplies, and other conditions which obtained at that time, such rates would no doubt be profitable. The board of railway commissioners have made a statement in that regard, and I think it well to remind the house of it. In its judgment of October 14, 1924, in the Crowsnest pass case, the board said:
The Canadian Pacific railway rates, as contracted for. by the agreement of 1897, while then fair and reasonable under then traffic conditions, are not adequate to present conditions of traffic, and do not furnish an adequate return for the service concerned, and are not fair and reasonable, representing as they do but 35 per cent to 60 per cent of rates found adequate under present traffic conditions.
That is the situation in which grain is moved to-day, at a rate which the board of railway commissioners have found represents only from 35 to 60 per cent of an adequate return.
There is no objection to moving grain for export at that rate. The railways have not protested and no one has protested. Why? To move grain for export in competition with other countries of the world more favourably situated as to geography, it is necessary to be able to move it at an extremely low rate; and that being recognized, the railways are willing to do their share. I have no doubt they accept the fact that, as this is necessary to the national economy, it is a desirable movement for the railways.
Railway Act-Grain Rates

We come now to the domestic rate, which is a movement within the country. I think it has always been accepted; I know it has always been accepted since railroading began, that there is a difference between the export movement, which is highly competitive with other countries, and the domestic movement of grain within the country. We find a differential existing in all of the large consuming centres of Canada as between the export rate and the domestic rate. The board of railway commissioners have examined the domestic rates for movements to British Columbia and have found them to be fair and reasonable; nevertheless the railways have, by agreement, introduced, voluntarily and without compulsion on the part of the board, a lower rate to move feed grains, that is, the lower grades of wheat, and coarse grains, destined for consumption in British Columbia. Again, they did that in the national interest. The agricultural industry of British Columbia is a matter of interest to all Canada, and the railways agreed to transport feed grains to that consuming population at a rate greatly reduced below the domestic rate. Having done that, they have made, I believe, a sincere attempt to satisfy the requirements of that area. As a matter of fact, this arrangement was made in settlement of the demand of the western provinces that the Crowsnest rate should apply on domestic grains. The offer was made by the railways, and accepted by the provinces, and I think we can regard it, remembering the circumstances of the arrangement, only as an agreement binding on both parties. However, the fact that this subject has been repeatedly brought up in parliament indicates that there may be a grievance, or if there is no real grievance, that a great many people believe they have one.
One thing that has been particularly stressed in the presentation of the case by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) is that the rate on mill feeds moving into British Columbia should be carried at the same rate as that which applies on the movement of feed grains. The hon. member gave the house a rather erroneous impression of the rate at which these mill feeds move. He gave the house the impression that they now move at the domestic rate from mill to consumer. This, of course, is not the fact, as those hon. gentlemen who are familiar with milling in transit rates must be aware. The mill feeds move from the farm to the mill on the
domestic rate for that particular haul, and then the flour and by-products move through to destination on the balance of the through rate. The balance of the through rate is, in some instances, lower than the feed grain rate; in some instances it is higher. In discussing the matter with the railways, I have expressed to them the opinion that the grievance or supposed grievance of the people of British Columbia is a matter that should receive consideration with a view toward removing the possible grievance.

Mr. Chairman, I have been seeking an opportunity, and here it is, to draw attention to some egregiously false information which was contained in a cable dispatch from London last summer with regard to the grading of apples. In this matter I certainly am not critical of the minister; rather do I seek his assistance, for the cable that I am going to read takes in vain the name of his director of marketing. It is a serious criticism of the trade commissioners of Canada and also a criticism of that portion of the fruit branch which has to do with inspection, upon which we in British Columbia rely to such a considerable extent and which we trust so well, because of their assistance in enabling the shippers and the producers to pay more and more attention to quality. The cable in question came from Mr. Grant Dexter, London correspondent of the Winnipeg Free Press, and was dated July 15. It reads as follows:
Dean A. M. Shaw, chief of the marketing section of the Canadian Department of Agriculture, and a group of senior officials of this department are finding plenty of reasons why Canada's exports are not growing as rapidly as desired. The conclusions are based on a two weeks intensive study of the British market. Out of their investigations here it is safe to predict will come a severe overhauling of the Canadian government's export grading regulations, and a tightening up of their enforcement. The inquiry has revealed that many Canadian products are not being shipped to Britain in the way required by this market. Tests made of shipments of canned goods and fresh fruits, notably apples, proved conclusively that inferior products are being sent here under Canadian top grades.
Canada's finest, upon examination, turned out all too often to be wretched goods which could not possibly qualify for high grades if the Canadian inspection service were adequate. Boxes of apples, with good fruit on top and bad underneath, occurred too frequently under close inspection of these officials to bring real satisfaction with the efficiency existing in the federal inspection service.

Naturally that caused considerable stir in British Columbia. I can tell the story I wish to tell most quickly by reading an exchange of letters which took place. On August 12,
I wrote the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) as follows:
I have just returned to the Okanagan after a short absence, and I find a stormy atmosphere consequent on some allegations, as to the quality of our fruit in the United Kingdom market, by Grant Dexter.
I am in fairly close touch with the situation at both ends, and if this condition prevails, it must have come about fairly recently.
The industry is taking the matter up with the Department of Agriculture and with Mr. Shaw, but I want you to tell me what your trade commissioners have to say, for if things have gone bad recently, they would have certainly reported it to you, and they can also bear out, or disagree with, my opinion that our stuff has, in recent years, reached the British market in very good condition. So, at least, I have been informed over there on frequent occasions, and it was certainly so considered at the time of the 1932 conference.
It is a very, very, serious statement and one which I think the government must take notice of. I enclose one of the many references to the matter in the valley papers.
The minister replied through his private secretary, and enclosed a copy of a letter which had arrived from the Canadian government fruit trade commissioner in London. I shall read one or two paragraphs of the letter from London, which is dated August 20, 1937:
In the first place there were no Canadian boxed apples on the market during the whole period of the delegation's visit to this country and therefore it was impossible for any member to make the inspections reported and there is not the slightest trace of truth in the published statements-"boxes of apples with good fruit on top and bad underneath, occurred too frequently under the close inspection of these officials." It is presumed that Mr. Dexter obtained information by interview, but I find it hard to believe that any member of the delegation made such a statement, it is really an accusation of deliberate fraudulent packing. Further, I know of no importer of repute in the United Kingdom who would have made such a statement to the member of the delegation responsible for reporting upon the fruit situation. I have been concerned with the Canadian fruit industry for many years and innumerable opportunities have occurred to examine boxed apples in the packing house and in the markets of the United Kingdom and Canada, and I can state with emphasis that my experience has been quite the reverse to that as reported by Mr. Grant Dexter.
I would say that there is not an atom of truth in the report on boxed apples as published by the Winnipeg Free Press and further there is no justification whatsoever for such a statement.
I have discussed this matter with Mr. F. Hudd-

He is Canadian trade commissioner for Canada in London.
-and he has had several conversations with Mr. Grant Dexter. I understand that Mr. Dexter realizes the error in his cabled dispatch and it occurred to me the best manner in which the matter could be settled was for Mr. Dexter to withdraw his dispatch.
At the same time the Minister of Trade and Commerce sent me a copy of a letter he had written to the Winnipeg Free Press, dated August 31, as follows:
Inasmuch as the dispatch from Mr. Grant Dexter published in the Winnipeg Free Press under date of July 15th was definitely inaccurate and could hardly fail to injure our export trade in the commodities mentioned, I feel it is only proper that you make some adequate correction.
I enclose for your information a copy of a letter which has been received from Mr. W. B. Cornell, Canadian Fruit Commissioner.
In a subsequent letter the Minister of Trade and Commerce sent me a copy of the second Grant Dexter cable. The cable is dated at London, August 19, and is headed "Bad fruit not sent from B.C." The text is as follows:
Cables and letters received here indicate that the British Columbia apple growers have drawn an unintended and unwarranted conclusion from your correspondent's dispatch of June 15 regarding inquiries by Dean Shaw and his associates into the quality of Canadian foodstuffs exported to this market.
The apples referred to as being found good on top and bad underneath did not come From British Columbia. It was never suggested that they did. I
I pause there to draw attention to the fact that not only were there no boxed apples in London at that time, but the boxed apples which reach London during the course of the year are 90 to 95 per cent British Columbia apples. The cable continues:
The apples and canned goods named by your correspondent were only examples of the food products shipped to this market and opened under the eyes of the Canadian officials which proved deficient in quality but all the Canadian apples shipped here did not come from British Columbia. Other products could have been cited.
Tightening of the expert grading regulations and an intensive educational campaign among Canadian exporters is regarded as' certain at the next session of the dominion parliament when full details of the departmental inquiries here will doubtless be given official form.
Regarding British Columbia apples, careful inquiry among the trade fails to uncover any complaints as to quality or packing.
The reply received from the Winnipeg Free Press by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, dated September 3, is as follows:
I beg to acknowledge your letter of August 31st, calling attention to the dispatch from 51952-168J
Supply-Agriculture-M arketing
Grant Dexter which appeared in the Free Press July 15th. Since then we have published a further dispatch from Mr. Dexter which expands the brief extract from it mentioned in the letter from Mr. Gornall. I think it has been made amply clear that there should be no unfavourable reflection upon boxed apples from British Columbia sold in the British market, and this forms in my judgment the "adequate correction" which you suggest.
I then wrote the Minister of Trade and Commerce on September 18. I first referred to the fact that he had sent me a copy of Grant Dexter's cable and Mr. Ferguson's letter, and then continued as follows:
The cable maintains the original assertion m a slightly modified form, that "food products shipped to this market and opened under the eyes of the Canadian officials" are "deficient in quality" and I hope that you will go over the head of the managing editor and obtain an honest retraction of a journalistic libel, published as prominently as the original falsehood.
I can assure you that the matter is by no means dead here, nor in the other fruit growing parts of Canada. The public has been told by a widely read journal that "boxes of apples, with good fruit on top and bad underneath, occurred too frequently under the close inspection of these officials." The statement is emphatically denied by the Fruit Trade Commissioner in Great Britain, and the evasive later comments of the correspondent read strangely but they are approved by the managing director.
The journalist is fond of telling us that all he wants is news, accurate news, and that he has as high a regard for ethics as has any other professional man. If the editor of the Winnipeg Free Press endorses that constantly reiterated view, he cannot fail to give proper denial to this falsehood.
The correspondence ends with the reply to that letter from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The letter, which is dated September 29, 1937, reads:
While I am inclined to agree with the thoughts expressed in your letter of September 18, I do not believe any good purpose could be served by going into this matter further with the Free Press. Possibly if you eared to ventilate this in the house it would do much more good.
I do so. I appeal to the minister for his assistance. This is an absolutely false statement. I assume that this man is a Canadian and that he has the confidence of the Winnipeg Free Press. I am ready to concede to the members of the press every desire to follow the ethics of their profession, just as I as an engineer try to follow the ethics of mine. Undoubtedly at times journalists will be in error as I have been in error as .an engineer. But over the course of years that I have been connected with the fruit industry the Winnipeg Free Press has never been ready to give accurate or reasonably fair

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
information with regard to the fruit industry, even in this country. For its special representative in London, presumably sent there because it has confidence in him, to send back such a cable as that, merely means that he is doing damage to a Canadian industry.
I only wish to state that Mr. Shaw, the director of marketing in the department, made a denial at the same time with regard to boxed apples from British Columbia.
That is very little to get from the minister.

I should like to ask the minister a question in connection with marketing in England. I have in my hand a report of an interview with the Hon. T. C. Davis of Regina in connection with his trip to Eng-

land to be present at the coronation. He refers to the wonderful experience he had, and in conclusion the report reads:
The speaker also dealt briefly with Britain's rearmament program and the fact British people were inclined to slight Canada's goods because Canadians were not making any contribution towards the defence of the country which is her greatest market, Britain.

Mr. SEN'N: I have in my hand a report entitled, The British Market and the Canadian Farmer. It is the report made by a committee which, I understand, was sent to Great Britain to study the marketing there of Canadian farm products, and was headed, I believe, by the director of marketing services, Mr. Shaw. It is a very interesting report indeed. It was released, I think, in the fall of 1937, and there is some story to the effect that it had been released for only a very few days when further distribution of the publication was suppressed. Mr. Chairman, as has

I think I can best answer the next part of the question submitted by my hon. friend by reading from the reprinted issue of that publication. It states the policy as announced at the meeting to which the hon. member referred, in these terms:
With the winding up of the schemes operating under the "Natural Products Marketing Act'" completed, the dominion Department of Agriculture has given careful consideration to the recommendations set forth in the report of its investigating committee and has decided upon a policy in relation to the market in the United Kingdom.
Under that policy the department proposes:
A.	To see that Canada sets her own house in order by cooperating with provincial departments to have production improved and developed in most favourable locations and by ensuring, as far as possible, that no merchandise unsuitable to that market be exported to the United Kingdom and that what is exported be improved in quality, packaging and labelling.
B.	To cooperate with producers, exporters, brokers and the trade in the United Kingdom in maintaining, until the product reaches the consumer, the standard of Canadian agricultural products in conformity with the grades, packaging and labelling provided by Canadian regulations.
C.	To advise, cooperate with and assist all government, producer and merchandising agencies in placing Canadian foodstuffs effectively before the British housewife.
I shall now develop these main recommendations in greater detail: A. A number of products are already in such a condition that the full story can be told about them-i.e., cheese, bacon and breakfast foods. A great deal of work is required with others, in particular canned goods and poultry.
1.	We propose that definite steps be taken to see that the fullest information about the character of the United Kingdom market be given to the producer.

All possible means should be employed to this end;-e.g., through provincial departments of agriculture, at conventions, by special meetings, by carefully prepared articles in the agricultural press, by the issue of special booklets, and by any other useful method. The aim of all this should be to- show the producer the severity and type of the competition he must meet, the particular requirements of the market, the necessity for meeting these requirements, the need for paying particular attention to such matters as labelling, and, in short, the necessity for doing his part in proving to the housewife and to the trade in the United Kingdom that the words "Canadian Product" always mean a reliable, quality product. We also feel that at every step the producer should be kept fully informed of what is being done to increase the demand for his product on the British market.
2.	We have had ample evidence that the grading of certain Canadian products has continued to improve. The matter is of such importance, however, that we feel it vital to stress the necessity of further careful attention to grading, particularly in regard to fostering, as far as possible, a standard, to all graders in every part of the dominion.
3.	The only proper basis on which the two main policies, (B) and (C), as outlined, can be carried out is by emphasizing the consistently high quality of Canadian products. Publicity for an inferior article is not only worth nothing, but is definitely harmful to all good products. We have considered very carefully whether it is advisable to prohibit entirely the export to the United Kingdom of all low-grade products. Such a prohibition, we feel, would entail a severe hardship upon individual producers, as there is a low price market in Great Britain which may be invaluable to the producer who, for instance, owing to unfavourable climatic conditions, has a large amount of low quality products.
It is essential, however, that more and more of our products should be of high quality so that agencies placing it on the market can maintain it in high favour. We therefore intend to advocate:
(a)	The adoption of a national mark for Canada's high grade agricultural- products shipped to the United Kingdom.
(b)	That the use of this mark be made compulsory on specified products provided they attain the requisite standard; that this mark be made the focal point of any publicity and advertising campaign; by this means the mark would assume a definite and valuable significance.
(c)	That the right to use this mark where it is not compulsory, be accorded only to producers under licence, provided that their products attain to the required standard to be laid down by the dominion Department of Agriculture.
(d)	That, with proper safeguards, the right to use the mark be accorded to United Kingdom importers or blenders who import Canadian products in bulk and package or blend them themselves.
(e)	That this mark be either an emblem or label, so designed, either by shape, colour or wording, or a combination of these, that it can be readily identified by the British housewife.
(f)	That sub-standard products have a distinctive mark.

B.	The dominion Department of Agriculture intends to follow, in relation to other products the practices pursued in relation to cheese and bacon which have met with good results in recent years.
C.	The dominion Department of Agriculture does not conduct advertising campaigns in Great Britain, and never has. The marketing service of the dominion Department of Agriculture will cooperate in every possible way with the publicity committee or any producer or merchandising agency interested in promoting the sale of farm products in the United Kingdom.

9.	Transportation as it applies to the handling of perishable products at Canadian docks is under investigation.
This is the difficulty that has always existed. Danish bacon is shipped in special boats built for the purpose and is loaded in a special way. Argentine beef is handled similarly. There the beef goes into cold storage at the wharf and is kept at a constant temperature as it crosses the wharf to the boat. It is at the same temperature in the boat, never varying more than one degree from the time it is put into cold storage until the time it reaches the market. We have no such service and with our present volume we could not have it. We have this experience, too, that much of our bacon is produced in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba, some of it being cured there, put into cold storage or

When the product reaches the dock, it is sometimes left for a time on the dock subject to heat, especially during the months of July and August, and is finally raised and put in the hold of a boat. In other words, it is subject to changes of temperature. The Transport department, the research council and the Department of Agriculture as well as the Department of Trade and Commerce are cooperating at the present time in conducting an investigation into ways and means of providing facilities at our docks from which bacon is being shipped, so that the bacon can be transferred from warehouse, or the car in which it is shipped to Montreal, to the boat without undergoing this great difference in temperature, which it experiences particularly in the two months to which I have referred. I am informed that the greater part of the difficulty, most of the complaint with regard to the quality of our bacon, has to do with shipments sent forward in July and August, largely because of that variation in temperature which takes place at different points.
The Department of Agriculture in cooperation with the national research council has the matter under consideration. This problem is one of great national importance, a satisfactory solution of which will have a very definite bearing upon the future development of Canada's trade in perishable products with Great Britain.

Is there any provision in these estimates for a staff apart from the supervision of the work of the people already over there.

Under the general
marketing vote for this division of the department we can make appointments to clerical positions, such as a secretary for the commissioner, and also other appointments under the provisions of the vote itself for any assistance he may require; but at the present time his staff is composed of about six men, I think, who have been in England representing the department for many years. I think the first appointment was made in 1912, and from that time down to the present additions have been made to the number. No new appointments were made by the present government until we appointed this last representative. He really takes the place of Mr. Wilson, who previously occupied a similar position in the department, and who a few years ago was transferred from the Department of Agriculture to the Department of Trade and Commerce. We are not undertaking the sale of farm products, but we are following those products through to the consumer. We are carrying on investigations as to the quality and grade of the product. We shall do that very much in the manner that investigations were made last year; that is, probably an individual will

The minister was just speaking about the high quality that w'ould be required in connection with goods sent to the United Kingdom, and he also made the statement that there might be some sub-standard products shipped to that market. That for the export of sub-standard products the word "empire" be substituted for the word "Canada" or that regulations be made limiting the size of type that may be used to show their Canadian origin.
It seems to me that is treading on rather dangerous ground.
That is why we changed it.

I know the minister has changed it to some extent, but I should like to know just how sub-standard products are going to be marked, if they are to be marked at all; or are they to go into the British market without any distinguishing features about them? If so, will the consumers know they are Canadian products and judge Canadian products accordingly? It seems to me most dangerous to have our first-class products marked Canadian and to send to the old country other Canadian products which may destroy the reputation which otherwise might

be built up. I should like to know just how these products are going to be marked, if they are going to bear any distinguishing Canadian mark, and I want to warn the minister that I am afraid it is a dangerous practice to follow.

I should like to direct the attention of the hon. member and the committee to the fact that the publication from which quotations are being read is the report of a committee. think it is important to know just how our bacon is being marked, whether only the highest grade will be marked as Canadian bacon, whether some latitude will be allowed, or how far down the grades are going to be marked as Canadian.

It took some little

The question raised is quite controversial. It is very difficult for a layman to determine when bacon is select and when it is one of the lower grades when the hog is still running around. Much of the grading that is done in Canada is done while the hog is still running around. I think I am right when I say that grading in Denmark is all done on the rail after the hog has been killed. It is much easier to determine whether or not a hog is select when you see it hanging up. A hog graded while still alive might be classed as select, and yet, when converted into bacon, it might be of a lower grade. It is difficult to say that the bacon from a hog which had been graded as select when it was still alive will be of that particular grade.
The figures indicate that there has been rapid progress in this country toward rail grading. The first criticism I had after coming into the department came from those who were opposed to this type of grading. They had heard a report somewhere that we were about to pass legislation enforcing rail grading. Their objection was that in a country like Denmark, where all the hogs are owned by a cooperative of the producers, where they are fed according to the regulations of the cooperative, where they are housed according to the regulations of the cooperative, where they are selected and, I believe, actually killed and marketed by the cooperative, it is easy to maintain a standard and to carry on rail grading without the producer himself suffering any disadvantage.
The first objection to enforcing rail grading in Canada at the present time is based upon the wide distribution of our people from one ocean to the other, the different conditions under which feeding is carried on, and more particularly the fact that if we are going to have this type of grading, all hogs will have to be slaughtered in a slaughter-house or abattoir. The producers maintain that they would rather take their chances on grading when the hog is running around the yard. I am not in a position to state definitely that we can adhere as closely to regulations with regard to selects as they are able to do in a country like Denmark. However, we are advancing rapidly toward the rail grading of hogs. They are all graded in that manner in the maritimes. I was looking up some statistics the other day, which I am sorry I have not with me to-night, and I was surprised at the rapid increase in the last three years in rail grading. If we continue at this rate we shall soon reach the point where we can have something of the kind suggested.

I should not like the committee to get the impression that I am agitating for rail grading and doing away with the present system. I was complaining that there was included in grade A these different weights to which I have referred. Whether they are rail graded or graded on the hoof makes no difference if you ensure that there will be in grade A only that weight of side which is considered to be the best for the British market. I referred to the five different grades of hogs to indicate the wide variety of sides that were included in grade A. This lack of uniformity is largely responsible for the ten to fourteen shillings difference in price in what is received for our bacon and Danish bacon. It is against that practice that I have been speaking this evening.	[DOT]

Has any progress been made in having the packers adopt a uniform system of processing in order to produce a uniform quality of bacon? A select hog may go into one packer and come out a certain grade, while a similar hog may go to another packer who is not using the same system of processing, and it comes out a different grade altogether. The minister stated that certain interests had agreed on this trade mark. Just who were those interests?

I am not in a position to state the concerns to which this trade mark was submitted. It had to be examined in relation to the trade marks of the different concerns that had already registered trade marks with the proper authorities. It was finally determined by council that this was the proper mark to indicate to people outside as well as in Canada that we considered it a quality product and one that could be depended upon.
In connection with processing, I think it will be admitted that each of the larger packing houses, as well as some of the smaller ones, maintain that they have the best process. They contend that they have been successful in producing a taste, if nothing else, for their bacon, which is preferred by a great many people. I doubt if we would succeed in attempting to have them all use exactly the same process, and I doubt very much if anything would be accomplished by doing that. The companies have a cooperative arrangement by which they exchange certain information as to the best methods of protecting themselves against deterioration of their products. I do not think there is any necessity for the government to do anything in the way of enforcing this, because it is recognized already by the companies that it is to their advantage to do so.

Supply*-Agriculture-Marketing

Could the minister give us the results of the investigation carried on by the Department of Agriculture to determine the grade of hog most suitable for rail grading and most likely to meet successfully the competition of Denmark?

All I say with regard to that is that any one travelling across Canada will realize that we have a national type of hog. The long Yorkshire type has been in this country for a number of years and it has been pretty well standardized all across Canada. The Yorkshire type is the prevailing type at our shows and it will be found in almost any farm yard. The department feels that it would be a mistake at the present time to discourage the farmers from continuing with that common type.

I should like to say one word more about this mark. It seems to me that this is one of the most important departures we have had for some time. It is particularly important in regard to the shipment of our bacon to the old country. Perhaps we get more benefit from the Ottawa agreement in the sale of our bacon in the old country than in the sale of any other product, and as an hon. member said a moment ago, it is regrettable that our bacon at the present time sells for so much less in the British market than bacon from any other country except perhaps the Balkan states. The. report I have in my hand, which we have been discussing, gives two or three reasons why our price should be and is lower, and, among others, the fact that there are. so many different grades of bacon going from Canada overseas. But, in addition, there is another statement made on page 33 of the report which is very important. It says:
Some of the larger wholesalers have made very definite representation in regard to the large volume of box cuts being shipped from Canada.
Further down it says:
37.107,089 pounds were shipped as hams, and 24,015,918 pounds were shipped as box cuts.
And again:
Wholesalers put forth the argument that the large quantities of Canadian cuts have a depressing influence on the price of Canadian Wiltshires.
I wonder if the mark is going to be put on hams and box cuts. That particular type of meat would be classed as No. 1; it seems to have a depressing influence on the price of our bacon in Great Britain, and the price we receive there undoubtedly settles, to some extent at least, the price of hogs in Canada.

So I think every effort should be made to see that we get the very highest price possible over there because it means money in the pockets of our farmers; but if we continue to send over these box cuts and picnic hams in ever increasing quantities, I do not know just what the result is going to be.
An answer to a question that was asked here by the member for York East (Mr. McGregor) shows that in 1935, 17,000,000 pounds of box cuts went over there; in 1936,
30,000,000 pounds; and in 1937, 35,000,000 pounds, in addition to a large increase in the volume of hams sent over there. While our export of Wiltshires is increasing as well, it is not increasing so rapidly as our shipment of these other cuts which are said to have a depressing influence on the market. I think the minister would be wise to see that steps are taken to have Wiltshire sides shipped in as large a volume as possible to the mother country. After all, I believe we have nearly enough select hogs produced in Canada to supply our trade with the mother country if they were all used for that purpose, and I believe they could all be used for that purpose. It is true perhaps that some of our own people would like the very best bacon that could be produced, but on the other hand I think nine out of ten would not know the difference between bacon produced from a bacon hog and bacon produced from a select hog. I am sure I would not myself. I think we should take the same steps which are being taken by Denmark and other countries to see that only the very highest quality is sent over there, and in as large a volume as possible. I would ask the minister if any steps are being taken to see that this is being done.
I would ask the minister one other question, which he might answer at the same time. If the mark is used, it will have to be very carefully guarded to see that nobody uses it on a product that should not be graded as No. 1. Is it the intention of the department to see that all goods which are shipped to the old country are graded by government graders, because it seems to me that is the only way in which we can carefully guard the mark to see that it is not improperly used?
Practically all the products that go to the old country now are graded by government graders, and it will be the intention to improve on any grading that is now being done.

They are graded only by
sample, I understand, at the present time, are they not?

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing

It would be impossible to grade every package that goes over or anything of that kind. That is the very reason why we have placed the commissioner in England, the very reason why we want this work supervised. We expect to check the product that goes to England much more carefully than we have done up to date, in connection with the grading and packaging and everything that has to do with it. If the mark is applied to bacon-and I would hope it will be-it will be done for the purpose of ensuring that as large a percentage as possible of the shipment of bacon to Great Britain will be of the very highest quality. That will be the objective of the department in everything that is done in connection with it, and I can assure the hon. member that it will be the objective in connection with all our farm products, including bacon, going to Great Britain.

The minister has stated that he has not finally decided what products will come under this mounted policeman's head. I hope that he will give the matter a great deal of consideration before he includes boxed fruit under it. I wonder if he would see fit to consult the industry, or at least to seek their opinion, before he makes his decision. I make that suggestion for this reason: For a considerable number of years now, boxed fruit of that description has been graded efficiently, I think. The shippers largely have their own brands which are established in the British and northern European markets, and it appears to me that it would be of assistance to the minister in arriving at his decision if he would first seek the opinion of these established shippers of boxed fruit.
There is no doubt that the shippers of all products which are being shipped will be consulted very fully before any decision is reached.

In reference to the
remarks made by the hon. member for Haldimand, the quality of the hogs raised in western Canada must naturally vary, and if we had a market for only our very best quality in Great Britain we should have to find a market for our other products. I know that in London the best hams are the Cumberland hams. That is a different type of pig from the Yorkshire, and I do not know whether there are any Cumberland hogs raised in this country. However, we know that changing economic conditions have made it very difficult for importing nations to import only the highest quality of goods, and I believe it is
important not only to grade the goods but to have an efficient sales force over there with a proper sentiment towards the English purchaser, and in sympathy with the British market. The commissioner would do more good by meeting these people who sell these products in the Smithfield market. I am speaking now as a person brought up in the old country, and I am looking at the matter from the point of view of marketing goods through personal services, because I believe that if the sales force is of the right type a good many of our difficulties would be ironed out. As a western farmer I realize what a tremendous quantity of hogs are sold at times that are probably slightly under the highest grade, and therefore we must develop a market for all types besides the very highest type of Wiltshire bacon.
Would the minister inform the committee what is the total cost of the report?

I have not the exact amount here. The cost was not very high; indeed it was low. The other day a question in regard to the matter was placed on the order paper, but I am not sure that it has been answered yet.
When was this report first sent out?
I think it was on December 8.

There is a matter which I wish to call to the attention of the committee, and I think it may well be done in connection with this marketing act. It has to do with our dairy business. I wish to call the attention of the committee to an extract from a speech made by the minister.
I wonder if the hon. member would allow that to come up under dairying, if it has to do with dairying.
It has something to do with marketing as well as with dairying.
There is a dairy vote. But it is all right.

The minister made this statement as reported on page 162 of Hansard:
The cheese producers of Ontario, with the assistance of the Minister of Agriculture of the Ontario government of that time, cooperating with the dominion government, sent their secretary over to England to advance the sale of cheese in that market.
I wish to point out just what have been the results of the cooperation between the department of agriculture of Ontario and the Department of Agriculture of the dominion.

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
The minister said further in that same address that in 1900 Canada produced 220,000,000 pounds of cheese and that in 1935 the production had fallen to 100,000,000 pounds; that in 1907 Canada sold to Great Britain 190,000,000 pounds but that in 1935 the amount sold had fallen to 52,000,000 pounds; and that in 1907 New Zealand had sold 27,000,000 pounds to Great Brtiain but in 1935 they had increased that amount to
197.000.	000 pounds. These figures are correct. But the minister said that when he saw those conditions he went over to England to examine into the marketing of Canadian cheese in the old country. When he arrived there, he said, Canadian cheese was not being advertised; he saw New Zealand cheese and Australian mutton and butter advertised, but no advertising of Canadian cheese. I might call his attention to the fact that in 1934 the Ontario government robbed Canada of the greatest advertising agency we had by closing Ontario House in London, where our goods were being advertised.
The impression that was left on the house by the remarks of the minister was that New Zealand had crowded Canada out of the British market. That is not so. New Zealand never crowded Canada out of the British market; Canada herself receded from that market. Great Britain bought our cheese and paid us a premium for all that we could supply her. The amount of cheese we sold in Great Britain was the amount of high quality cheese that we could produce. There was a sale for it there if we could produce it. We must take into consideration the different conditions. One thing the minister did not tell us was that, while our cheese sales to Great Britain had diminished to that extent, the production of dairy products in Canada had increased very rapidly; that our milk production was rapidly increasing and was being consumed in other lines.
New Zealand has a population of about
1.600.000,	almost entirely rural. One of her principal exports is cheese. Canada has a population of 11,200,000 with over fifty per cent of them residing in the urban centres, non-producers of agricultural products. While New Zealand's principal export is cheese, Canada makes cheese only out of her surplus milk. No cheese factories will be found around our large centres as cream, whole milk, butter and ice cream are required to supply the demand. One has to go into backward places removed from the great industrial centres before one finds a cheese factory. In fact, as I heard one prominent dairyman say the other

day, in Canada cheese was always looked upon as a poor relation of the dairy business; it got what was left over. That is a fact. We are large consumers of whole milk. We are one of the largest consumers of butter in the world. We consume large quantities of cream, and people are using more cream than they ever did before; one might instance the ice cream trade. When all those demands are supplied we make our surplus into cheese, and Great Britain has been paying us a premium on it. We have had no trouble in selling it; there was a ready market for it there. Fifty per cent of all the milk produced in Canada is going into butter; we are making into cheese only eight per cent of the milk we produce. To indicate the extent of the increase in the consumption of butter, we are making to-day in Canada 69,000,000 pounds more butter annually than we were making ten years ago and consuming practically all of it ourselves; in fact, this year we have imported large quantities of butter to supply our own local demands. Of all the dairy products produced in Canada, 93i per cent are consumed by the Canadian people; we export only 64 per cent.
Let us consider the difference in the manner in which New Zealand cheese and Canadian cheese are handled on the British market. New Zealand sends her cheese in consignments, in large shiploads. It is put into cold storage in London, Liverpool, Glasgow and other large cities; she has her agents there selling that cheese on commission, and they are advertising it.
Government agents?

Yes. Cheese is being handled there cooperatively by the New Zealand government and they are selling that cheese on commission; they are out advertising it. But Canadian cheese is sold by cable in Canada before it leaves this country. Our cheese is not sold in Great Britain except by retail; it is sold in this country before it leaves our shores, and it goes into the hands of the trade in that way. Great Britain as I have said, pays us a premium on that cheese.
What I wish to call to the attention of the committee is that the cooperation which has been taking place between the Ontario department of agriculture and the dominion Department of Agriculture has not been in the best interests of the dairy business, because they have been directing their efforts to the selling end of the business, the cheese being sold on its merits, and have neglected the producing end of it. Those of us who

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing
are connected with the dairy business know full well that we have individual cows which are producing from twenty to twenty-five thousand pounds of milk a year. We have many dairy herds which are producing individually between ten and fifteen thousand pounds of milk. But the average dairy cow in the Dominion of Canada produces less than five thousand pounds. While we cannot all have these high producing cows, there is. far too much difference between the possible and the actual. That is where the quantity comes in. Then there is the quality to be considered.
Let me now refer to the report that has already been discussed to-night. I want to show what these men have to say with regard to cheese. On page 42 I find the following:
Canada's success in marketing cheese in the United Kingdom depends upon the quality of the product, and every possible effort should he made to improve the quality still further. . . . Continued effort should be put into the endeavour to improve the quality of cheese. . .
This report is correct. Our goods were sold on their quality and a premium was paid for them. Our problem was to produce goods of that high quality and there was a ready market for them. In 1934, when the present Ontario government came into office, they found an organization known as the Eastern Ontario Dairymen's Association which had been in operation for sixty years and had built up that great dairy business of eastern Ontario, where the largest percentage of high grade cheese has always been manufactured. They were getting a provincial grant of $1,500 at that time:, but the then provincial minister of agriculture, Mr. Duncan Marshall, saw fit to withdraw it. A deputation from the dairymen's association, comprising some of the outstanding dairymen in the province, waited on him, and he assured them that in future the farmers would have to pay their own shot; that there was no more government money to be put into the industry. That was that. What he did was this: We had at that time a few small organizations known as cheese producers' associations, and they got behind an effort to organize one in every county. There had been some of them before that. They organized a cheese producers' association for the province of Ontario, so that they had a central organization for Ontario and smaller county organizations. These are organizations of producers which can do splendid work in the dairy business. I have no fault to find with them in any way; but they were badly led; their activities have not been directed along the proper channels.
They have been directing their efforts towards selling a product that was sold on its merits, and have neglected the producing and quality.
After the grant was withdrawn and the association which had built up a great industry was put out of business, the Ontario department passed an act permitting the Cheese Producers' Association of Ontario to assess five cents per 100 pounds against all cheese sold in the province. In 1936 this association collected directly from the farmers $22,000. Last year they collected $38,671, and the Department of Agriculture of the dominion made them a further grant of $5,000. They employed a secretary at Belleville to whom they paid $3,000 and expenses, and they sent a man to England, giving him $5,000 and expenses. This man at Belleville bought a few thousand boxes of cheese and shipped them to England, and the man there peddled them around London. That was one of their activities. The other one was this-they held a convention.
Before I go into that, I would call attention to a statement made by the minister, and I think it was a very timely one. He drew the attention of the committee to the small quantity of cheese being consumed by the Canadian people. Let me put on record the per capita consumption of cheese in a number of countries: Switzerland, 23 pounds; Holland, 14f pounds; France, 13i pounds; Denmark, 13i pounds; Italy, 12 pounds; Germany 11| pounds; Britain, 9J pounds Scandinavia, 7 pounds; New Zealand, 4i pounds; United States, 4f pounds; Canada, 3f pounds. We have Canada and New Zealand, two of the largest producers of cheese, with the smallest per capita consumption. I know nothing of New Zealand; but so far as Canada is concerned, I think this small consumption is our own fault. With a slight increase in the home consumption of cheese and we would have little to export. What is the trouble? We are great consumers of butter. Go into any hotel or restaurant and the waiter will put a piece of butter on your plate, and if you use it, give you another piece. They replenish your supply. Did you ever see them put a piece of cheese on your plate? If you asked them for a piece they would give you a small, little sample which you could put into your mouth all at once. If we used cheese on the table as we use butter, we would double the consumption. The people are not eating cheese, because they cannot eat what they do not get. Quite a large sum of public money has been expended in a way

The Late Mr. Betts

which in my humble opinion has not been in the best interests of the dairy business. I have before me the auditor's report for the cheese producers' association of Ontario. As I have already told the committee, they were engaged in two activities. One was buying cheese in Canada and sending a man over there to sell it, trying to break up a cheese buying and selling organization of which this country is justly proud and which New Zealand would like to have.
